guide.title: About the Dashboard
guide.p1: The Dashboard is your main overview page. It displays your most recent speed test results, bandwidth history charts, and any featured monitoring agents at a glance.
guide.p2: From here you can quickly review trends in your network performance over time and share results with others.
guide.li1: The performance history chart shows download, upload, and ping trends over a selected time range (1H, 6H, 24H, 7D, 30D, or All).
guide.li2: Click 'View Details' on any test result to see full metrics for that specific test.
guide.li3: Use the Share button to generate a public link for sharing your results.
guide.li4: You can pin monitoring agents to this dashboard from the Agents tab.

guide.title: About Speed Test
guide.p1: The Speed Test tab lets you measure your network's download speed, upload speed, and ping latency using various server protocols including Speedtest.net, LibreSpeed, and iperf3.
guide.p2: Select a server closest to you for the most accurate results, or choose a distant server to test international connectivity.
guide.li1: Speedtest.net servers use the standard protocol and are widely available worldwide.
guide.li2: LibreSpeed servers are self-hosted alternatives using an open-source protocol.
guide.li3: iperf3 servers allow raw TCP/UDP throughput testing â€” great for LAN and datacenter testing.
guide.li4: Use the Schedule Manager (Advanced section inside Server Selection) to automate tests at regular intervals or specific times.
guide.li5: Results are saved and shown in the Dashboard tab for historical analysis.

guide.title: About Trippy (Continuous Traceroute)
guide.p1: Trippy performs a continuous, real-time traceroute â€” similar to the classic MTR (My Traceroute) tool â€” giving you live per-hop statistics as long as it runs.
guide.p2: Unlike a one-shot traceroute, Trippy keeps probing each hop repeatedly and accumulates statistics, making it ideal for diagnosing intermittent issues and identifying unstable network paths.
guide.li1: Enter any hostname or IP address (e.g. 8.8.8.8 or google.com) and click Start.
guide.li2: Each row in the table represents one router hop on the path to your destination.
guide.li3: Loss% shows the percentage of probes that did not receive a reply â€” high loss at a single hop is not always a problem if subsequent hops respond normally.
guide.li4: Jitter is the variation in round-trip time â€” high jitter indicates an unstable connection.
guide.li5: The chart at the top shows how latency evolves over time for each hop.
guide.li6: Click Stop to halt continuous tracing.

iranTools.title: Iran Tools
iranTools.description: A set of network tools curated for Iran's internet situation: check which sites are reachable, find clean CDN edge IPs, test SNI-based filtering, and modify VLESS configs.

protocolChecker.title: Protocol / Port Checker
protocolChecker.description: Checks which protocols and ports are currently connectable from your network — HTTP/HTTPS, CDN alternate TLS ports, DNS variants, QUIC/HTTP-3, SSH and more. Results reflect your city/region and ISP conditions.
protocolChecker.durationTooltip: All probes run concurrently; the total time is roughly the slowest single test (about 6 seconds max).
protocolChecker.noData: No data yet. Run a check to see which protocols and ports are connectable from your network.

guide.title: What does this tool do?
guide.p1: It probes dozens of common protocols and ports simultaneously from your current network: raw TCP connects, real TLS handshakes on Cloudflare's alternate ports, the DNS family (UDP, TCP, DoT, DoH), QUIC/HTTP-3 over UDP, and SSH.
guide.p2: Results are only valid for the network you are on right now — port blocking and filtering differ between cities, provinces and even ISPs, which is why the detected location is shown alongside the results.
guide.li1: The CDN alternate TLS ports (2053, 2083, 2087, 2096, 8443, 8883) are the same ports usable by VLESS/Trojan configs behind Cloudflare — if one is blocked, try another.
guide.li2: If QUIC/HTTP-3 passes, outbound UDP on port 443 works and clients using that transport can rely on it.
guide.li3: If plain DNS/UDP is blocked but DoH/DoT pass, switch your client to encrypted DNS.
guide.li4: The latency shown is connection setup time; run the check a few times in a row to judge stability.

domainChecker.title: Domain Checker
domainChecker.description: Scan popular domains to see which ones are currently accessible from your network.
domainChecker.customDomainTooltip: Add any domain you want to test in addition to (or instead of) the built-in list of popular sites.
domainChecker.usingDefaults: No custom domains added â€” the built-in list of popular domains will be scanned.
domainChecker.usingCustom: {{count}} custom domain(s) will be scanned instead of the default list.
domainChecker.noData: No data yet. Run a scan to see which domains are accessible.

guide.title: What does this tool do?
guide.p1: This tool tries to open each domain in the list over HTTPS and reports whether a valid response was received. If a domain times out, resets the connection, or fails the TLS handshake, it is marked as Blocked.
guide.p2: Use the custom domain field to test specific websites you care about, such as a service you use for work.
guide.li1: Accessible: the site responded normally â€” it is very likely reachable in your browser too.
guide.li2: Blocked: the connection failed or timed out â€” this usually indicates DNS, IP, or SNI-based filtering.
guide.li3: Latency shown is the time to receive the first response; high values may indicate throttling rather than outright blocking.

edgeScanner.title: Edge IP Scanner
edgeScanner.description: Scan IP ranges to find clean, unfiltered CDN edge IPs (e.g. Cloudflare) that respond correctly for a given domain.
edgeScanner.sniRequired: Please enter a domain/SNI to test against
edgeScanner.rangesRequired: Please provide at least one custom IP or CIDR range
edgeScanner.sniTooltip: The hostname used for the TLS handshake and HTTP request while scanning. It must be a domain served through the CDN whose IPs you are scanning (e.g. a Cloudflare-protected site).
edgeScanner.rangeTooltip: Choose the official Cloudflare IP ranges, or provide your own list of IPs/CIDR ranges â€” useful for scanning Akamai or any other CDN's ranges.
edgeScanner.customRangesPlaceholder:
One IP or CIDR range per line, e.g.
104.16.0.0/24
172.64.100.5
edgeScanner.concurrencyTooltip: How many IPs to test at the same time. Higher values scan faster but use more resources and bandwidth.
edgeScanner.noData: No data yet. Start a scan to search for clean IPs.

guide.title: What does this tool do?
guide.p1: This scanner connects directly to each IP address in the selected range using TLS with the given domain as the SNI, then sends an HTTP request with that domain as the Host header. If a valid response comes back, the IP is considered 'clean' for that domain/CDN.
guide.p2: This is useful when your ISP blocks a CDN's main/anycast IPs or blocks by SNI/DNS, but individual edge IPs in the CDN's range still work.
guide.li1: Use the Cloudflare preset to scan Cloudflare's official IP ranges â€” works for any Cloudflare-protected domain (the default example uses ChatGPT's domain, but you can use any Cloudflare site).
guide.li2: Use custom ranges to scan any other CDN (such as Akamai) â€” paste the IP ranges you want to test.
guide.li3: Working IPs found here can typically be used in VLESS/VMess/Trojan configs by replacing the server address, as long as the SNI/Host stays set to the domain you scanned with.
guide.li4: Lower the concurrency if your connection becomes unstable during scanning.

sniSpoof.title: SNI Spoof Check
sniSpoof.description: Check whether SNI-based filtering can be bypassed on your network by spoofing (fronting) the TLS SNI with an allowed domain.
sniSpoof.fieldsRequired: Please fill in both the target domain and spoofed SNI
sniSpoof.targetDomainLabel: Target domain (the one you want to reach)
sniSpoof.targetDomainTooltip: The domain that may be blocked. The tool will request this domain's content using the Host header while hiding it from SNI-based inspection.
sniSpoof.spoofedSniTooltip: A domain that is definitely NOT blocked on your network. Its name is sent in the unencrypted TLS handshake instead of the real target domain.
sniSpoof.ipTooltip: Optional. If left empty, the target domain's own IP address will be resolved and used automatically.
sniSpoof.resultOpen: SNI spoofing works â€” filtering can likely be bypassed
sniSpoof.resultOpenDesc: The server accepted the spoofed SNI and returned a valid response for the target domain. This suggests your network filters by SNI only, and traffic can be disguised behind an allowed domain.
sniSpoof.resultClosedDesc: The connection failed, was reset, or did not return a valid response. Either the target IP does not serve this domain, or filtering happens at a deeper level than SNI alone.

guide.title: What does this tool do?
guide.p1: Many filtering systems inspect only the unencrypted 'Server Name Indication' (SNI) field during the TLS handshake to decide whether to block a connection. This tool tests that theory by connecting to the target's IP while sending a different, allowed domain name as the SNI, then requesting the real target domain over the now-encrypted connection.
guide.p2: This is a diagnostic tool only â€” a successful result does not automatically configure anything, it simply tells you whether this bypass technique is viable on your current network.
guide.li1: Pick a spoofed SNI that belongs to a large provider sharing infrastructure with your target (e.g. a domain behind the same CDN).
guide.li2: If the target domain uses a CDN, try pairing this tool with the Edge IP Scanner to find a good IP first.
guide.li3: Results can vary between networks/ISPs and may change over time as filtering rules are updated.

vlessModifier.title: Vless Config Modifier
vlessModifier.description: Replace the server address in a VLESS config with a list of alternate IPs to quickly generate multiple ready-to-use configs.
vlessModifier.invalidLink: Could not parse this VLESS link. Make sure it starts with vless:// and includes a host and port.
vlessModifier.noIps: Please provide at least one valid IP address or IPv4 CIDR range
vlessModifier.linkTooltip: Paste your existing vless:// link here. Only its server address will be replaced; the UUID, port, and all query parameters (like SNI) are kept as-is.
vlessModifier.ipsTooltip: One IP address or IPv4 CIDR range per line (or comma-separated). CIDR ranges are expanded into individual IPs, capped at 500 total configs.
vlessModifier.ipsPlaceholder:
One IP or CIDR range per line, e.g.
104.16.100.1
172.64.100.0/28
vlessModifier.truncatedWarning: The IP list was truncated to the first 500 addresses to keep things responsive.

guide.title: What does this tool do?
guide.p1: Many VPN/proxy providers give you a single VLESS link, but connecting through a different server IP (while keeping the same UUID, port and SNI) can sometimes yield much better speed or bypass filtering. This tool automates creating one config per IP.
guide.p2: Everything runs locally in your browser â€” your VLESS link and generated configs are never sent to the server.
guide.li1: Find candidate IPs first using the Edge IP Scanner tab (make sure the SNI you scanned with matches your config's SNI).
guide.li2: Paste single IPs, or a CIDR range like 172.64.100.0/28 to generate a config for every address in that range.
guide.li3: Test the generated configs in your VPN client and keep the ones with the best speed and stability.

guide.title: About Traceroute & Network Monitors
guide.p1: The Traceroute feature maps the network path from the server to any destination, showing each router (hop) along the way with three round-trip time measurements.
guide.p2: Network Monitors run continuous ICMP ping or MTR checks against a target at scheduled intervals, recording packet loss and latency over time.
guide.li1: Enter a hostname or IP, or pick one of the available servers to trace the route from that location.
guide.li2: Each hop shows three RTT (Round-Trip Time) measurements â€” variations indicate unstable routing.
guide.li3: A '*' (timeout) means that router did not respond to probes â€” this is common and does not always indicate a problem.
guide.li4: Switch to Network Monitors to set up continuous monitoring with alerts for packet loss exceeding your threshold.
guide.li5: MTR-based monitors provide richer per-hop statistics compared to simple ICMP ping.
guide.li6: Monitor results are stored historically so you can review past network quality.

guide.title: About Agent Monitor
guide.p1: The Agent Monitor tab lets you connect to and monitor remote machines running the Netronome agent. Each agent reports live bandwidth, CPU, memory, disk usage, and system information.
guide.p2: Agents are lightweight processes you install on any server or machine you want to monitor. They communicate back to this dashboard over HTTP.
guide.li1: Click 'Add Agent' to register a new agent by entering its URL and optional API key.
guide.li2: The Overview tab shows live bandwidth speed, CPU/memory/disk usage at a glance.
guide.li3: The Bandwidth tab shows historical traffic charts over time.
guide.li4: The System & Hardware tab shows detailed OS, CPU, memory, disk, and temperature information.
guide.li5: You can 'feature' up to 3 agents on the Dashboard for quick monitoring at a glance.
guide.li6: Agents that are offline will show their last known cached data.
